title: Southern Baptist Convention advances amendment targeting women pastors
text:

FILE - Messengers stand for worship during a Southern Baptist Convention annual meeting Tuesday, June 11, 2024, in Indianapolis. Delegates to the Southern Baptist Convention's annual meeting voted Wednesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would exclude churches from the denomination if they affirm, appoint or endorse women serving as pastors.
The amendment passed by a vote of 6,028 to 2,026, easily surpassing the two-thirds threshold required for constitutional changes. Delegates will have to approve the measure again at the convention's 2027 annual meeting in Indianapolis before it officially becomes part of the SBC constitution. The amendment states that cooperating Southern Baptist churches may not act "to affirm, appoint, or endorse a woman serving in the office or function of a pastor/elder/overseer, specifically preaching to the assembled congregation.
" The vote marks the latest development in a years-long debate within the nation's largest Protestant denomination over the role of women in church leadership. Supporters say the amendment clarifies and strengthens the SBC's long-held beliefs regarding pastoral leadership. Critics argue it further limits opportunities for women who feel called to ministry.
"We're incredibly disappointed that Southern Baptists continue to try and make women in ministry their top priority when there are so many other things that need to be addressed," Stone told NBC 15 News. Stone noted that previous efforts to amend the constitution faced hurdles despite advancing through the convention process.
"This year's amendment was actually different because it was even more strict than the previous wordings of those amendments," she said. "It is one that they were able to get passed through, and now it will come up again next year to be put into effect. " Ahead of the vote, Baptist Women in Ministry launched a billboard campaign in Orlando carrying the message: "God calls women to pastor, preach, and minister.
" Stone said the organization's goal was not necessarily to change the outcome of the vote, but to encourage women who may be struggling with questions about ministry and calling. She said the campaign was designed to reach women who may feel isolated within the debate.
"It was our hope that women who may be struggling in silence as they are a part of the Southern Baptist Convention, or those who may be sensing an inkling of a call, would see that and it would stay with them and be an encouragement to them," Stone said. "There were so many women who reached out and said, 'Thank you so much for speaking up on our behalf,'" she said.
Stone acknowledged that many women remain committed to Southern Baptist churches despite disagreements over the issue.
"Sometimes people say, 'Why don't Southern Baptist women just leave? ' Well, it's a lot more complicated than that," Stone said. "This is their faith home, the place where they met God and want to follow God's calling. Leaving is not that simple.
" The debate is particularly relevant in Alabama, where Baptists make up the state's largest religious group. According to the Public Religion Research Institute, roughly 42% of Alabamians identify as Baptist. As the amendment heads toward a final vote next year, Stone said she hopes church members focus on what she sees as the broader mission of ministry.
"There are so many things in our world that are worthy of our attention that are harming people physically, emotionally and spiritually," Stone said. "Why would we limit the workers who could go out into the world and build the beloved community of God?
"If approved by a second two-thirds vote at the 2027 Southern Baptist Convention annual meeting in Indianapolis, the amendment would become part of the denomination's constitution and could lead to the removal of churches that continue to affirm women serving in pastoral roles.
